title: A Redis channel carrying more than one proto/events/v1 envelope type could be silently misdecoded
what_happened: While building gateway's WebSocket layer (T7) - the first actual consumer of delivery-worker's Redis channels - it became clear that room:{room_id} carries both ChatEvent and MatchingEvent's MatchEnded, and user:{account_id} carries both MatchingEvent's MatchFound and ModerationEvent's AccountBanned (DEC-0067's own routing table), but delivery-worker republished the original Kafka bytes with nothing identifying which envelope type they were (DEC-0067's 'republish verbatim' choice).
impact: No user-visible impact yet - gateway had not been built far enough to actually consume these channels. Caught before any real traffic could hit it, not in production.
root_cause: ChatEvent, MatchingEvent and ModerationEvent all declare event_id at field 1, occurred_at_unix at field 2, and their own oneof starting at field 3 - all three identical in shape at the wire level. protobuf's wire format carries no type tag of its own, so proto.Unmarshal does not error when given bytes from the wrong message type; it silently produces a structurally valid but wrongly-interpreted result. This was missed when DEC-0067 decided to republish Kafka bytes unchanged, since at that point nothing yet read the ambiguous channels to expose the problem.
resolution: Every Target.Payload delivery-worker publishes is now one tag byte (1=ChatEvent, 2=MatchingEvent, 3=ModerationEvent - router.EnvelopeKind) followed by the original bytes, documented in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.5 since gateway (a separate Go module) implements the same convention independently rather than sharing a constant across module boundaries. Verified with updated unit tests asserting the exact tagged byte sequence, and the existing real-Kafka-and-Redis integration test re-run successfully against the new format.
lessons: A design decided before its consumer exists needs re-checking once that consumer is actually built, not just trusted - the ambiguity was invisible by construction until something tried to tell two message types apart on the same channel. Any wire format shared across two separate Go modules needs its own explicit documentation (here, in ARCHITECTURE.md), since the type system can't enforce agreement the way a shared Go package would.

title: A one-byte envelope-kind tag resolves the Redis channel type ambiguity, instead of a schema registry or separate channels
context: INC-0009 found that a Redis channel can carry more than one proto/events/v1 envelope type with no way for a consumer to tell them apart from the bytes alone.
options: Separate Redis channels per envelope type (e.g. room:{id}:chat and room:{id}:matching), so a subscriber knows the type from which channel a message arrived on
Wrap every published message in a small common outer envelope (a new proto or JSON wrapper carrying a type field plus the original bytes)
Prepend one raw tag byte identifying the envelope type, before the original bytes
decision: One tag byte (router.EnvelopeKind: 1=ChatEvent, 2=MatchingEvent, 3=ModerationEvent) prepended to the original Kafka message bytes, unchanged otherwise.
rationale: Splitting channels by type would mean a WebSocket connection subscribing to multiple channels per room/account instead of one, complicating the subscription bookkeeping DEC-0067 already settled on, for a problem that's really about telling 3 known, fixed cases apart - not a cost a general solution (a schema registry, a new wrapper message) is worth paying for. One byte is the smallest possible encoding of '1 of 3 known kinds' and needs no additional parsing step beyond slicing it off before the existing proto.Unmarshal call.
tradeoffs: The tag is a convention maintained by hand in two separate Go modules (delivery-worker and gateway) rather than a shared, compiler-checked type - documented in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.5 specifically because nothing else enforces the two sides agreeing.

title: Gateway's JWT and WebSocket libraries: golang-jwt/jwt/v5 and coder/websocket
context: DEC-0014 and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4.3/§5.2 specify an HMAC-signed session JWT and a WebSocket protocol, without picking concrete libraries - the same kind of gap T6 already resolved for Kafka and Redis by checking actual repository activity rather than memory (DEC-0061).
options: golang-jwt/jwt/v5 vs the older, now-archived dgrijalva/jwt-go for JWTs
gorilla/websocket vs coder/websocket (the actively maintained continuation of nhooyr.io/websocket) for WebSockets
decision: github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5 v5.3.1 and github.com/coder/websocket v1.8.15.
rationale: Checked each candidate's actual repository state: golang-jwt/jwt had a commit the day before this check and a January 2026 release. gorilla/websocket's last release was June 2024 and its last commit March 2025 - over a year stale as of this decision - while coder/websocket (which Coder explicitly took over maintaining from nhooyr in 2024, per its own README) released v1.8.15 in June 2026. Both libraries' go.mod files declare a Go version compatible with this project's 1.27.2 (DEC-0051).
tradeoffs: None of real consequence for either choice at this project's scale.

title: HTTP error responses map gRPC codes the same way grpc-gateway does, verified against its source
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.1 specifies the error body shape ({error: {code, message}}) and that HTTP status codes are 'mapped from gRPC codes', but not the exact mapping.
options: Invent a mapping by judgement call
Adopt the mapping github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway's runtime.HTTPStatusFromCode already uses, verified by reading that function's actual source
decision: internal/httpapi.httpStatusFromCode reproduces grpc-gateway's HTTPStatusFromCode mapping exactly (codes.NotFound -> 404, codes.PermissionDenied -> 403, codes.ResourceExhausted -> 429, and so on through every code grpc-gateway handles).
rationale: This mapping is already a de facto standard used by a widely-adopted project for exactly this purpose - reusing a verified, battle-tested mapping is strictly better than inventing an equivalent one from scratch and risking a subtle mismatch (e.g. guessing codes.Aborted maps to 409 Conflict, which it does, but is not the obvious first guess).
tradeoffs: None - this is a pure lookup table with no behavior to trade off.

title: A WebSocket connection refreshes its room subscriptions by polling ListMyRooms, not an event of its own
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.1 and §5.2 split room creation/joining (HTTP: POST /v1/rooms, POST /v1/rooms/join) from live delivery (WebSocket, subscribed to Redis's room:{room_id} channel per §5.5) - but define no WebSocket client frame or Redis signal telling an already-open connection 'you just joined a new room over HTTP, start listening to it'.
options: Add a new WebSocket client frame (e.g. room_subscribe) the client sends right after a successful HTTP join
Have the gateway instance that served the HTTP join somehow signal the same account's open WebSocket connection directly
Periodically re-fetch Chat.ListMyRooms and diff against the current subscription set
decision: Every WebSocket connection calls Chat.ListMyRooms once at connect and again every 25 seconds (reusing the client's own documented ping cadence as the timer, rather than running a second one), subscribing to any new room:{room_id} channels and unsubscribing from any it's no longer in.
rationale: The first option needs a new protocol frame docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 doesn't define, and the client would have to remember to send it. The second needs a cross-instance signal that only works if the HTTP request and the WebSocket connection happen to land on the same gateway instance, which isn't guaranteed once this is horizontally scaled. Polling is simple, needs no protocol change, and a 25-second worst-case delay to start receiving live events for a just-joined room is an acceptable cost at this stage - DEC-0071 in the same sense that pragmatic polling choices elsewhere in this project (DEC-0045's presence heartbeats) accepted similar latency for similar simplicity.
tradeoffs: Up to 25 seconds between joining a room over HTTP and this connection's first live event for it. A newly joined room's invite acceptance itself is still synchronous (the HTTP response confirms membership immediately) - only the live delivery is delayed, not the join itself.

title: match_end acts on a room id tracked from match_found/match_ended, since its own client frame carries none
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 lists match_end's client-to-server fields as 'none', but ending a direct room (Chat.EndDirectRoom) needs a room_id, and Chat has no 'end my current room, whichever it is' RPC.
options: Change the documented protocol to add room_id to match_end (a breaking change to an already-agreed section)
Have the gateway connection track its own 'current direct room' from the match_found and match_ended events it has already observed over Redis, and use that for a bare match_end
decision: Each WebSocket connection keeps a currentMatchRoomID, set when its own redisLoop translates a match_found event and cleared on match_ended, guarded by a mutex since one goroutine writes it and another reads it. match_end and match_next both use this tracked value.
rationale: This keeps the documented client protocol exactly as specified rather than silently diverging from it, and the information is already flowing through the connection anyway - every account's gateway connection necessarily observes its own match_found before it could ever be in a room to end.
tradeoffs: A connection that reconnects after a match was found but before any match_ended arrives starts with no tracked room until the next match_found/match_ended - reconciling that from Chat.ListMyRooms on reconnect (already fetched for DEC-0073's room-subscription refresh) is a reasonable future improvement, not implemented here.

title: keep_status's own-vote response reports You unconditionally but Partner only when the room is actually kept
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2's keep_status frame has you/partner/kept fields, but Chat.VoteKeep's response (DEC-0031) only reports whether the room is now kept overall, not each member's individual vote.
options: Guess partner's vote state when not kept (e.g. always report it as false)

Report you=true (this connection just voted, so this is always known for certain) and partner=kept (if the room is now kept, the partner must also have voted; if not, partner's status is genuinely unknown from this response alone, so it is reported as false rather than guessed at as a confident negative)
decision: The synchronous response to a keep_chat frame reports {you: true, partner: resp.kept, kept: resp.kept}.
rationale: partner=false when not kept is not asserting the partner voted no - it's the only value available without a dedicated RPC for per-member vote state, and is clearly correct in the one case where it can be confirmed (kept=true implies the partner's vote happened too).
tradeoffs: A client reading partner=false after voting can't distinguish 'the partner hasn't voted yet' from 'nothing more is known' - acceptable since the UI's only real decision point is whether the room survived (kept), not the partner's exact vote timing.

title: Gateway refuses to start without SESSION_SIGNING_KEY, unlike Google sign-in's optional degrade
context: Identity's own pattern for optional configuration (COLLEGE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID unset) is to log a warning and fall back to a Disabled verifier that rejects just that one feature, keeping the service running. Gateway's session signing key has no equivalent optional feature to disable instead - sessions are load-bearing for every authenticated endpoint.
options: Mirror identity's pattern: warn and fall back to some default behavior
Generate a random ephemeral key at startup when unset, accepting that every restart invalidates all existing sessions
Refuse to start
decision: main.go calls log.Fatal if SESSION_SIGNING_KEY is empty. deploy/helm/service/values/gateway.yaml sets an explicit, obviously-fake placeholder value for local development, the same pattern deploy/k8s/dev/postgres.yaml's postgres-dev-credentials already uses.
rationale: There is no 'degraded but running' mode for a service whose entire job is authenticating every other call it makes - a missing signing key is a configuration error worth learning about immediately (a crash-looping pod) rather than a service that starts, appears healthy, and silently fails every authenticated request, or worse, one that silently rotates its signing key on every restart.
tradeoffs: None - this is strictly safer than any degraded alternative for a required piece of configuration.

title: Manual live-cluster verification of gateway used a stale delivery-worker image that predated the envelope-tag fix
what_happened: Verifying gateway's WebSocket layer end-to-end on a real kind cluster (working around a Tilt/kind interaction that had made tilt ci unreliable in this environment - see the WIP branch history) meant building and loading images by hand instead of through Tilt. delivery-worker was reused from an existing locally-cached Tilt image (tag tilt-11285f1c26b0ba51) rather than rebuilt, since it hadn't changed in this branch's own work. A real send_message over the WebSocket got its message_ack but the live message frame never arrived; gateway logged 'unknown envelope kind 10'.
impact: No user-visible impact - caught during manual pre-merge verification, never reached a real deployment. Delayed finishing gateway's verification by the time it took to diagnose and rebuild one image.
root_cause: Byte value 10 is the raw protobuf wire tag for field 1 (events_v1's event_id), not router.EnvelopeKind's ChatEvent tag (1) - proof the cached image was built from before INC-0009/DEC-0070's one-byte envelope tag landed on main (PR #14), even though main itself has carried the fix since. Reusing a cached image by its content hash silently skipped a fix that a fresh build from current main would have included.
resolution: Rebuilt delivery-worker from current main (docker build -t flamingo/delivery-worker:verify), loaded it into the kind node, redeployed, and re-ran the same manual WebSocket flow - the message frame arrived correctly on retry. Confirmed end-to-end: guest signup, WebSocket auth, room creation, send_message's synchronous message_ack, and the live message frame delivered back through Kafka, delivery-worker and Redis.
lessons: A cached image is a snapshot of whatever main was when it was built, not a proxy for 'main hasn't changed this service lately' - any manual verification step that bypasses Tilt's own build-from-source-every-time behaviour needs to rebuild every image it uses, not just the ones under active development, or it can validate against code that's already been superseded.

title: The matching queue is one atomic Redis script per attempt, with two sorted sets selected by the seeker's own preference
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.2 agrees the shape (an atomic Redis script scanning the oldest 100 waiting candidates, dropping entries older than 10 minutes) but leaves the actual key layout and algorithm open ("algorithm Proposed").
options: One global waiting pool, filtering every candidate by gender in Lua on every scan
Two pools: mq:any (everyone waiting, for preference=any seekers) and mq:want:{gender} (verified waiting users indexed by their own actual gender, for gender-restrictive seekers to scan directly)
decision: mq:any always gets every waiting account regardless of its own preference; mq:want:male/mq:want:female additionally get an account only when it is itself verified with that gender. A seeker's own preference picks which one pool it scans (ARGV, not KEYS, for the per-candidate mq:entry:{id}/avoid:{id} keys the scan only discovers at runtime). Mutual compatibility - does the candidate's own preference also accept the seeker - is then checked in Lua against the candidate's stored preference/gender/verified fields.
rationale: Letting the pool choice do the seeker's half of the filtering (by construction, not a runtime check) keeps the script's actual branching to just the candidate's half (mutual acceptance) plus the previously-agreed staleness and avoid-set rules. Building a candidate's own entry/avoid keys from its id inside the script rather than declaring them as KEYS up front is safe only because this project's Redis is a single instance, never a cluster where key-to-node routing would require every key declared in advance - documented here since it departs from the stricter convention gateway's ratelimit script follows for its one, statically-known key.
tradeoffs: A candidate whose own preference is any is visible to every seeker, including ones its own gender wouldn't otherwise qualify for under a gender-restrictive seeker's filter - correct per §3.2's mutual-acceptance rule, but means mq:any is not merely 'a pecking-order-free version of mq:want:*', it is the superset every account always joins.

title: A match:members:{room_id} Redis cache lets Next re-enqueue the caller, since match_next's client frame carries no attributes of its own
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 already agrees match_next's client frame has no fields ("none (end the current random chat and queue again)"), but RequestMatch's TryMatch needs preference, gender, verified and pseudonym to look for a new match, and Matching doesn't call Identity itself for these (DEC-0014's trust boundary: the caller - gateway - supplies them, Matching doesn't look them up).
options: Change the agreed WebSocket protocol to add fields to match_next
Have gateway's already-shipped handleMatchNext call Identity.GetAccount itself and pass the attributes through a new NextRequest field, matching how handleMatchRequest already works
Cache both matched accounts' attributes in Matching itself when the room is created, keyed by room id, and read (then delete) that cache on Next
decision: RequestMatch's own tryMatchAndRoom helper saves both sides' Candidate as a pairing.Side pair under match:members:{room_id} right after CreateDirectRoom succeeds. Next looks the caller's own side up by current_room_id, uses it to re-run the same matching algorithm (with PreviousPartner set to the other cached side, so the same pairing isn't immediately repeated), and deletes the entry once consumed.
rationale: The first two options touch an already-merged, reviewed contract (the WebSocket protocol, or gateway's PR #15) for a problem that is really Matching's own to solve - it already has everything needed to cache this at the one moment (match creation) it's naturally available, with no new field or cross-service call required.
tradeoffs: match_end (§3.2's other way a direct room ends) calls Chat.EndDirectRoom directly from gateway, bypassing Matching entirely (DEC-0074) - so a room only ever ended that way leaves its cache entry with nothing to delete it. A 24-hour TTL bounds this as a safety net rather than a correctness requirement, since it's just a cache for re-enqueue convenience, not a source of truth Chat or anyone else reads. If Next's cache lookup misses (expired, or the account doesn't match either cached side), NextResponse.Queued is false rather than an error - the room still ends correctly either way, and the client is left to send a fresh match_request.

title: Next ends a direct room through Chat.EndDirectRoom, the same call gateway's match_end already makes, rather than producing MatchingEvent's MatchEnded
context: proto/events/v1's MatchingEvent has a MatchEnded payload (room_id, account_id), and delivery-worker's router already routes it to room:{room_id} with gateway's translate.go already computing a per-viewer you_left/partner_left reason from it - all built in earlier PRs ahead of Matching actually existing. Matching could either produce this event itself when Next ends a room, or just call Chat.EndDirectRoom the same way gateway's own match_end handler already does (DEC-0074), which produces ChatEvent's RoomEnded instead (a literal reason string, not per-viewer).
options: Next produces MatchingEvent_MatchEnded directly, in addition to or instead of calling Chat.EndDirectRoom
Next calls Chat.EndDirectRoom(reason: "next") - the same RPC and the same resulting ChatEvent_RoomEnded path match_end already uses - and never produces MatchingEvent_MatchEnded
decision: Next calls Chat.EndDirectRoom directly, exactly like match_end. MatchingEvent's MatchEnded, and its routing/translation in delivery-worker and gateway, are not produced by anything in v1.
rationale: Chat owns the rooms table and is the only thing that can actually mark a direct room ended (set ended_at) - Matching has no database of its own and must call Chat regardless of which event it also produces, so reusing the exact path match_end already ships keeps both ways a direct room ends consistent with each other rather than giving Next a richer, differently-shaped notification than End gets for what is, from either participant's side, the same kind of event.
tradeoffs: MatchingEvent_MatchEnded's per-viewer you_left/partner_left framing (richer than RoomEnded's single literal reason string) goes unused in v1 - the proto message, delivery-worker's routing for it, and gateway's translation for it all remain in place since removing them would mean touching two other already-merged services for a cosmetic pass outside this PR's scope, not because they're expected to be wired up later without a reason to.

title: handleMatchNext sends a match_queued frame on success, mirroring handleMatchRequest
context: Live verification of Matching (T8) was the first time match_next was ever exercised end to end against a real deployment. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 gives match_next no documented server-to-client response of its own, and gateway's already-merged handleMatchNext (PR #15) sent nothing back on success - but handleMatchRequest already sends match_queued unconditionally on success (RequestMatchResponse.Queued is always true per its own doc comment), so the two otherwise-parallel 'join the queue' paths behaved inconsistently: a client that called Next had no way to tell 'ended and re-queued' apart from 'ended and now stuck', since the room ending (match_ended, from Chat's own RoomEnded broadcast) and having rejoined the queue are two separate, independent facts.
options: Leave it as documented (match_next has no fields and no response) - a client infers re-queuing happened from NextResponse.Queued being unreachable to it, or just assumes it
Send match_queued after Next only when NextResponse.Queued is true, matching handleMatchRequest's existing pattern exactly
decision: handleMatchNext now sends a match_queued frame when Matching.Next reports Queued: true, and sends nothing when it reports Queued: false (DEC-0078's graceful degradation when there is nothing cached to re-enqueue with) - the client still learns the room ended from match_ended in that case, just not that it was also re-queued, since it wasn't.
rationale: This is the same information handleMatchRequest already gives a client for the exact same underlying fact (an account is now waiting in the queue); there is no reason Next's path should be less informative than Request's for the same event, and nothing in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 forbids an additional server-to-client frame type that's already documented and already sent by another flow.
tradeoffs: None of consequence - match_queued was already a defined frame type sent by the sibling code path.

title: Presence stores one Redis sorted set per category, cleaned lazily on read, and broadcasts counts on its own 5-second timer
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.4 (DEC-0045) agrees the shape - batched heartbeats, a sorted set per category scored by last-heartbeat time, entries older than 45 seconds dropped, counts published to Redis every 5 seconds - but not the concrete implementation.
options: One sorted set for everyone, storing the category as part of the member value and filtering in application code when counting
One sorted set per category (presence:guest/male/female/verified_other), so a count is a plain ZCARD with no filtering
decision: Four fixed keys, one per presencev1.Category. GetLiveCounts (and the 5-second broadcaster, which calls the same store method) first ZREMRANGEBYSCORE's each set below the 45-second cutoff, then ZCARD's it - lazy cleanup on read, the same pattern services/matching/internal/queue already uses for its own 10-minute staleness rule. CATEGORY_VERIFIED_OTHER is counted into Total only, matching GetLiveCountsResponse's actual fields (total/guests/male/female - there is no separate 'verified' field for the proto comment's 'counted in the total and in verified' to populate, so this decision also documents that half of the comment as not reflected in the message as it stands).
rationale: Four small, fixed-key sorted sets make every read a single ZCARD with no application-level filtering or scan, and the 5-second broadcaster's own periodic Counts() call means cleanup happens continuously whether or not anything ever calls GetLiveCounts directly - the same reasoning DEC-0077 used for the matching queue.
tradeoffs: A category with heavy churn does slightly more Redis work per read (one ZREMRANGEBYSCORE before every ZCARD) than a pure ZCARD would, acceptable at this project's scale.

title: Gateway tracks connected accounts in a per-process registry for Heartbeat, and forwards the presence channel over each connection's existing pubsub
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.4 assigns gateway two jobs that didn't exist in the already-merged Gateway PR (#15): sending one batched Heartbeat per instance every 15 seconds for every connected account, and forwarding the presence channel's live counts to every connected browser as the already-documented presence frame (§5.2). Building Presence without also doing this would ship a service nothing ever feeds data to.
options: A dedicated connection registry holding the *conn values themselves, for both heartbeat batching and (later) graceful shutdown

A lightweight registry holding only account id -> category, separate from the connections themselves; each connection keeps subscribing to Redis exactly as it already does for user:{account_id} and room:{room_id}, just with one more fixed channel (presence) added to the same pubsub
decision: internal/presence.Registry (gateway-side, distinct from the Presence service) maps account id to category, Set on successful auth and Remove deferred alongside the existing pubsub cleanup. One RunHeartbeatLoop goroutine per gateway process (started in main.go, not per connection) snapshots it every 15 seconds. Separately, authenticate's existing pubsub also subscribes to the fixed presence channel (a second Subscribe+Receive round trip, not combined with the user:{account_id} one, so each is unambiguously confirmed on its own rather than relying on SUBSCRIBE's multi-channel acknowledgements arriving in request order) - redisLoop checks msg.Channel and forwards presence messages directly as a presence frame, bypassing translate.go's envelope-kind path entirely since this channel is plain JSON, never a tagged proto/events/v1 envelope.
rationale: A full connection registry (the first option) is real future work - main.go's own shutdown comment already flags graceful WebSocket close as unimplemented - but Heartbeat only needs account id and category, not the connections themselves, so building the heavier registry now would be solving a problem (graceful shutdown) this change doesn't need to solve. Reusing each connection's own existing pubsub for the presence channel, rather than inventing a separate shared subscription mechanism, keeps exactly one pattern (per-connection Redis subscription, translated frame, enqueue) for everything a connection receives.
tradeoffs: A reconnecting account's second connection racing the first's cleanup could have its Set overwritten by the first connection's deferred Remove - accepted as a narrow gap in a count docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.4 already treats as a non-durable, eventually-consistent approximation, self-correcting within one heartbeat interval.

title: Gateway enforces bans by checking Redis's banned set on every authenticated path, and only writeLoop ever force-closes a connection
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.5 says gateways check the banned set on sign-in, on WebSocket connect, and on every send, and close a banned account's connections once kicked arrives - none of which existed yet (Moderation itself didn't exist before this PR). Building Moderation's BanAccount without this would ban an account in name only.
options: Check banned only at WebSocket connect and HTTP sign-in, relying on the kicked event alone for an account banned mid-session
Also check on every send_message and every withAuth-wrapped HTTP request, and have the kicked event actually close the connection, not just notify the client
decision: A small internal/banned package (SISMEMBER on "banned") is checked in: ws.authenticate (connect), httpapi.withAuth (every authenticated HTTP request, covering Google sign-in's resolved account and everything else in one place), httpapi.handleAuthGoogle specifically before issuing a session (a sign-in can resolve to an existing, already-banned account), and ws's handleSendMessage (every send). Separately, the already-translated kicked frame (AccountBanned, existing since T6/T7 but never actually disconnecting anyone) now gets closed by writeLoop specifically - the one goroutine that calls c.ws.Write, so it's the only place that can be sure the frame actually reached the client before the socket closes. handleSendMessage's own banned check only sends an error frame, deliberately not closing the connection itself, to avoid a second, racier close path.
rationale: Centralizing the actual close in writeLoop avoids the race a close call from redisLoop (right after enqueueing) or from handleSendMessage would have against the frame still sitting in the send channel, unwritten.
tradeoffs: A banned account's in-flight connection isn't forcibly closed by handleSendMessage's own check - it relies on the kicked event (already published by BanAccount) to actually disconnect it, which is near-immediate in practice but not synchronous with the rejected send.

title: Moderation's own design: mutual avoid sets on block, an upserted ban row, and Identity.AdminSetGender called only on approval
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.5 agrees the shape (reports, blocks populating avoid:{account_id}, bans populating the banned set) but not the implementation, and the proto's RequestGenderChange/ResolveGenderChangeRequest pair needs something to actually decide: does approving a request call Identity itself, or just record the decision?
options: BlockUser adds only the blocker's own avoid entry (one-directional)

BlockUser adds both directions (DEC's own reading of §3.5's literal wording: 'adds each account to the other's avoid set') so neither side is ever suggested to the other regardless of who blocked whom
decision: BlockUser's sets.AddMutualAvoid adds each account to the other's avoid set. BanAccount upserts one row per account in Postgres's bans table (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, clearing any previous unban fields), so a re-ban after an unban reuses the same row rather than erroring or duplicating history. ResolveGenderChangeRequest records the decision in moderation's own table always, and additionally calls Identity.AdminSetGender only when approving - Moderation is the only service with an Identity client for this one purpose, the same pattern Matching being the only service with a Chat client for CreateDirectRoom already set. Every admin RPC (ResolveReport, BanAccount, UnbanAccount, ResolveGenderChangeRequest) also writes one row to admin_actions, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6's 'who, whom, why, when, outcome' log.
rationale: Mutual avoidance matches a real safety expectation - a blocked person shouldn't keep seeing the person who blocked them either, pending symmetry aside. Upserting the ban row keeps one account's entire ban history in one place instead of growing an unbounded table of ban/unban pairs for repeat offenders.
tradeoffs: None of real consequence.

title: Blocking someone does not end an already-open direct room with them in v1
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.5 says 'the gateway ends the current random chat between them' when a block happens. Chat's Room message (chat.v1) carries no member list, and ListMyRooms returns rooms with no indication of who the other member is, so nothing - Moderation or gateway - can currently identify which of a blocker's open direct rooms (if any) involves the account just blocked, without first adding member visibility to Chat's contract.
options: Add member_account_ids to chat.v1.Room (additive) and have gateway's POST /v1/blocks handler look up and end the matching room via the same EndDirectRoom call match_end and Next already use
Ship BlockUser/avoid-set population now (which already prevents all FUTURE matches with the blocked account) and leave ending an already-open room with them as a known, documented gap
decision: Shipping without the automatic end-current-chat behavior. Blocking still immediately prevents any future match via the mutual avoid sets (DEC-0084); only an already-open direct room with the blocked account, at the moment of blocking, is unaffected until it ends some other way (Next, End, or the room simply not being kept).
rationale: The proto change and the gateway lookup logic it would require are real, contained work, but touch Chat's already-merged, reviewed contract for a safety nicety that's secondary to blocking's main effect (no future rematching) - taking the least committal option and logging the gap rather than scope-creeping this PR further (AGENTS.md's build-phase rule 8).
tradeoffs: A user who blocks their current direct-room partner must still manually leave (Next or End) to stop talking to them right now - a real, if narrow, safety gap worth closing in a follow-up.

title: banned_by/resolved_by/actor_account_id columns were typed UUID, but tools/admin's operator is not a real identity account
what_happened: Manual live-cluster verification of Moderation called BanAccount with banned_by set to a plain identifier string ("verify-script"), which failed with a Postgres UUID syntax error - these columns (bans.banned_by/unbanned_by, reports.resolved_by, gender_change_requests.resolved_by, admin_actions.actor_account_id) had been typed UUID on the assumption that whoever calls an admin RPC is a real identity account.
impact: No user-visible impact - caught during manual pre-merge verification, never reached a real deployment. Every admin RPC (BanAccount, UnbanAccount, ResolveReport, ResolveGenderChangeRequest) would have failed against any real tools/admin caller, since nothing in this project gives admin operators their own identity accounts.
root_cause: moderationv1's own proto fields (banned_by, resolved_by, etc.) are plain strings with no stated connection to identity.v1.Account; the Postgres schema (written ahead of tools/admin, which doesn't exist yet) incorrectly assumed they would always be valid account UUIDs, copying the pattern used for account_id columns that genuinely are identity accounts (reports.reporter_account_id, blocks.account_id, admin_actions.target_account_id).
resolution: Changed the affected columns to TEXT in migrations/0001_create_moderation.up.sql (not yet merged, so no new migration version was needed) and documented the distinction in the schema's own comments. Re-verified live: BanAccount, UnbanAccount, ResolveReport and the gender-change-request flow all work with an arbitrary, non-UUID actor identifier.
lessons: A column holding an id-shaped value isn't necessarily a foreign key to another table's real primary key - checking what actually produces that value (here, an admin tool that doesn't exist yet and has no defined identity) before choosing its type would have caught this without needing a live database to reject it.

title: tools/admin is a plain stdlib-flag CLI calling Moderation only, with each command's logic separated from flag parsing for testability
context: DEC-0050 already decided tools/admin is a command, not a service, calling Moderation and Identity from inside the cluster - but not its concrete shape: a framework or stdlib flag, one flat command set or subcommands, and whether it talks to Identity directly or only through Moderation.
options: A third-party CLI framework (e.g. cobra) for subcommand routing and flag parsing

The standard library's flag package, one flag.FlagSet per subcommand, with the actual logic in a separate internal/cli package taking an io.Writer and a narrowed ModerationClient interface so it's testable without flags or a real connection
decision: Plain flag.FlagSet-per-subcommand in main.go (reports list/resolve, ban, unban, gender-requests list/resolve), delegating to internal/cli functions for the actual work. tools/admin only dials Moderation - it never calls Identity directly; approving a gender change request goes through Moderation's own ResolveGenderChangeRequest, which calls Identity.AdminSetGender itself (DEC-0084). Every mutating command requires a -by flag naming whoever is running it, passed straight through to Moderation's own admin_actions log.
rationale: No service in this repo uses a CLI framework yet, and this tool's command set is small and fixed enough that stdlib flag costs nothing in flexibility while adding zero new dependencies. Only ever calling Moderation (never Identity) keeps the trust boundary DEC-0084 already established - Moderation is the one service with an Identity client, for exactly the admin-approval purpose - rather than this tool needing its own, separate copy of that same relationship.
tradeoffs: None of real consequence at this project's scale.

title: A message sent right after a match could be permanently missed by the other side, not just delayed
what_happened: Building tests/e2e's first scenario (two guests matching, then immediately chatting) against a real deployed cluster: the side that didn't send the message never received it, even waiting well past docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2's documented 25-second room-subscription refresh window (DEC-0073).
impact: No user-visible impact yet - caught by the new end-to-end smoke test before this behavior was ever exercised in a real deployment outside manual testing. Would have affected every real pair of users who matched and then one side messaged within roughly the first 25 seconds, for as long as this went unnoticed.
root_cause: match_found is delivered over a connection's existing user:{account_id} subscription, but nothing then subscribed that connection to the new room:{room_id} channel - only refreshRooms's periodic 25-second tick (DEC-0073's own accepted gap, written for a different case: a room joined over HTTP, which has no live signal to react to) would eventually add it. Unlike that case, Redis pub/sub has no replay for a new subscriber - a message published to room:{room_id} before the subscription exists is not delivered late, it is simply never delivered to that connection. DEC-0073's own text already says as much ("nothing is lost, only a live notification might be") but that reasoning covered the room's durable state being re-fetchable via Chat's API, not this specific live-delivery channel's own messages, which have no such durable fallback until persistence-worker's own write lands.
resolution: trackMatchRoom (internal/ws/dispatch.go) now subscribes the connection to room:{room_id} immediately when it processes a match_found frame, instead of waiting for the next refreshRooms tick - the connection already has a live signal to react to (match_found itself), unlike DEC-0073's HTTP-join case. Verified with a new integration test publishing a message to the room immediately after match_found, with no sleep or retry budget, so a regression back to the old behavior would fail outright rather than just run slow. The end-to-end smoke test that found this now passes consistently.
lessons: A documented, accepted latency for one case (a live event with no hook to react to) doesn't automatically justify the same latency for a superficially similar case that does have one - the two needed to be told apart, and only running the real flow against a real deployment (not a fake-backed unit test, which never exercises real Redis pub/sub timing or its lack of replay) actually surfaced the difference.

title: tests/e2e is a new, e2e-tagged module driven against a real Tilt stack, not part of CI's per-PR module matrix
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §11 calls for an end-to-end smoke test module covering four flows, run against Tilt - but CI's existing per-PR pipeline (DEC-0051/0052) only builds and tests individual service modules in isolation, with no live Postgres/Redis/Kafka/gateway stack to run this kind of test against.
options: Add tests/e2e to CI's module matrix anyway, accepting that go test ./... there would just find no buildable files without the e2e tag and pass vacuously
Add it to go.work (for local tooling - gofmt, go vet across the repo - to see it) but leave it out of CI's hardcoded module list entirely, documenting that it's run manually against a live stack
decision: tests/e2e is a separate Go module, added to go.work, every file tagged `e2e` (including its own TestMain). It is not added to .github/workflows/ci.yml's module list - docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §11 already frames this as driven against Tilt, which CI's current pipeline doesn't stand up.
rationale: A CI job that can never actually exercise this suite (no live stack) would be pure overhead - a green check that proves nothing, unlike every other module in the matrix.
tradeoffs: This suite's correctness is on whoever changes gateway, chat, matching, presence, moderation or identity to also run it manually against a live `tilt ci` stack before merging - nothing automated enforces that yet. A CI job that stands up a live stack and runs this suite is real future work (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §12's deployment pipeline is itself still 'to be designed').

title: tests/e2e's admin-tool scenario execs the real tools/admin binary; its report/block/ban scenario uses a verified reporter to stay within the guest-signup rate limit
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §11 says the report/block/ban flow goes "through the admin tool" specifically. Go's internal-package visibility rules mean tests/e2e (a separate module) cannot import tools/admin/internal/cli directly even in workspace mode - and independently, this suite's guest accounts (2 for matching, 2 for the group room, 2 more for report/block/ban) would total 6, one over the 5-per-hour-per-IP guest-signup limit (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4.4) every single run, not just on repeats.
options: Import tools/admin's cli package directly (blocked by Go's own internal-package rule, not a matter of preference)

Build and exec the real tools/admin binary as a subprocess, and reduce one scenario's guest-account count by using a verified (Google-fake-verifier) user instead of a second guest where the flow doesn't specifically need one
decision: tests/e2e/admin.go builds tools/admin once (go build to a temp dir) and execs it with real arguments for every admin action this suite takes, asserting on its real stdout and exit code - the actual deployable artifact, not its internals. TestReportBlockAndBanThroughAdminTool's reporter is a verified user (verifiedGoogleUser, which doesn't touch the guest-signup limiter at all) rather than a second guest, keeping this suite's total guest signups at exactly 5, not 6. A TestMain also resets this suite's own rl:guest_signup:* counters before running, the same kind of self-cleanup the service-level integration tests already do by truncating their own Postgres tables.
rationale: Execing the real binary is both the only option Go's visibility rules allow and the more faithful one anyway - it proves the actual thing an admin would run works, flags included. A verified reporter avoids inventing any special-cased rate-limit exemption or bypass for test traffic, which would be a change to production-facing safety behavior just to make a test's bookkeeping convenient.
tradeoffs: This suite's guest-account budget has no headroom - any scenario added later that needs a guest will have to also claw back a signup somewhere else (as this one did) or push the total over 5.

title: web/ uses plain React Context + useReducer for app state and no router library, with its own client-side pseudonym generator
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §10 specifies the screens (auth, random, channels, inbox) but not a state-management or routing approach. The app has three top-level screens switched by simple user action, no deep-linkable URLs, and no nested route trees - Random/Channels/Inbox behave more like tabs in a single-page app than independently navigable pages.
options: A router library (e.g. react-router) mapping each screen to a URL
Redux or another external state store for session/room/message state
Plain React Context + useReducer for state, and a bare state variable (not a URL) to pick the active screen
Import services/identity/internal/server/pseudonym.go's generator logic directly into the frontend
decision: web/src/state.ts holds one AppState behind a useReducer, exposed through web/src/gateway.tsx's GatewayProvider/useGateway context. Screen switching (web/src/App equivalent) is a plain state value, not a router. web/src/pseudonym.ts reimplements the two-word pseudonym generator independently in TypeScript, matching the Go version's style but not importing it.
rationale: Three tab-like screens with no deep links don't need URL-based routing - a router would add a dependency and a layer of indirection for no behavior this app needs yet. useReducer plus Context is already in the standard library and is enough for this state shape (one WebSocket connection, one account, a handful of in-memory collections); Redux would be another dependency doing the same job. The pseudonym generator can't be imported across the Go/TypeScript boundary, so it has to be reimplemented - matching the Go version's word-list style keeps guest pseudonyms visually consistent even though the two implementations can drift independently over time.
tradeoffs: No URL-based deep linking (e.g. a shareable link straight into a specific room) - acceptable for now since no screen needs to be shareable, but would require adding a router later if that changes. The two pseudonym generators (Go and TypeScript) can diverge silently since nothing keeps them in sync beyond this note; a mismatch would only be cosmetic (different word lists), not a correctness bug, since the frontend's generated pseudonym is just a local guess until the backend's own auth_ok response arrives with the real one.

title: The gateway had no CORS support at all, undiscovered until the first real browser frontend hit it
what_happened: Building and running web/ against a real deployed gateway for the first time, every HTTP request from the browser (guest signup, getMe, etc.) failed - the browser blocked them as cross-origin (the Vite dev server on :8000 calling the gateway on :8080), since the gateway sent no Access-Control-Allow-* headers at all.
impact: No production impact - no browser client existed before this point in the build. Every prior verification of the gateway's HTTP API (unit tests, integration tests, tests/e2e, manual curl and grpcurl calls) used a tool that doesn't enforce CORS, so the gap was invisible until a real browser was actually used, which is also the lesson.
root_cause: services/gateway/main.go wired its http.ServeMux directly into http.Server with no CORS-handling middleware anywhere in the request path. The WebSocket upgrade path (internal/ws) already checks Origin for its own reasons (cross-site WebSocket hijacking protection), which masked the fact that the plain HTTP API path had no equivalent check or allowance at all.
resolution: Added services/gateway/internal/httpapi/cors.go, a small middleware wrapping the mux that sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers for allowed origins and answers OPTIONS preflight requests with 204. It reuses the exact origin-matching semantics internal/ws already uses for WebSocket's own Origin check (path.Match against the WS_ORIGIN_PATTERNS list, read from coder/websocket's own accept.go source rather than assumed), so both paths now agree on which origins are allowed. Verified first with curl -X OPTIONS showing the correct headers, then re-confirmed against the real browser frontend.
lessons: A backend API with no real client yet has a blind spot that no amount of curl/grpcurl/Go-client testing will find: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, so nothing short of an actual browser request exercises it. The gateway's own WebSocket path already had equivalent Origin handling for a different reason, which is what made the plain-HTTP gap easy to reuse the fix for once found, but also what made it easy to overlook until something actually needed it.

title: GoogleSignInButton clears its container DOM node on effect cleanup, to stay correct under React StrictMode's dev-mode double-invoke
context: Google Identity Services' renderButton(container, options) appends a button into the given DOM node rather than replacing its contents, and nothing about the GSI script itself is aware of React's render lifecycle. React 19's StrictMode (on by default in development) mounts, cleans up, and re-mounts every component once as a deliberate check for effects that aren't safely re-runnable. The first version of this component rendered two Google buttons stacked on top of each other in dev, confirmed by a before/after screenshot comparison - cleanup existed but didn't undo renderButton's DOM append.
options: Leave it - the double-render is dev-only (StrictMode doesn't run in production builds) and cosmetic
Guard renderButton with a ref flag so it only ever runs once per component instance, ignoring StrictMode's remount
Make cleanup actually undo what the effect did: clear the container's contents on cleanup, so a remount renders into an empty node again
decision: The effect captures containerRef.current into a local const (also fixing an oxlint exhaustive-deps warning about reading .current during cleanup) and the cleanup function sets container.innerHTML = '' before the effect is allowed to run again.
rationale: StrictMode's mount-cleanup-mount is a real, intentional check that other effects in this codebase (e.g. the WebSocket connection in gateway.tsx) already have to be safe under - special-casing this one component to ignore it would leave an inconsistent standard, and the underlying bug (cleanup not undoing the effect's own side effect) is the same class of bug StrictMode exists to catch, not a StrictMode quirk to work around.
tradeoffs: None identified - clearing the container is a correct no-op on a production single-mount lifecycle (there is nothing to clear the first time) and the only thing that makes a second mount correct.

title: refreshRooms silently unsubscribed every random match's room about 25 seconds after it started, permanently killing live delivery for both sides
what_happened: Trying the web frontend end-to-end for the first time outside scripted testing (two real browser windows, a real random match, a real back-and-forth conversation), messages stopped arriving on both sides part way through a chat - not just for the other person, but even a sender's own message never came back over the live channel either. The first couple of messages right after matching worked; everything after some tens of seconds of being connected did not, consistently, on a fresh gateway pod with no errors logged anywhere.
impact: Every random (1:1) match would go live for roughly the first 25 seconds after match_found and then go permanently silent for the rest of that connection's lifetime, for both participants, with no error surfaced to either client or logged anywhere server-side - the exact failure mode a maintainer or a real user would describe as "the chat just stopped working" with no visible cause. Channels (group rooms) were unaffected. Caught during the first unscripted manual walkthrough of the merged web frontend (T11, PR #21), before any real user saw it.
root_cause: services/gateway/internal/ws/conn.go's refreshRooms runs every 25 seconds (readLoop's ping-interval ticker) and re-syncs this connection's room:{room_id} Redis subscriptions against Chat.ListMyRooms's current answer, unsubscribing anything no longer in that list. services/chat/internal/store's ListRoomsForAccount (confirmed by its own test, TestPostgresListRoomsForAccountReturnsGroupAndKeptDirectOnly) deliberately reports only group rooms and direct rooms both sides have already voted keep_chat on - an active random match is neither, for as long as it stays undecided, which is the normal state for the first messages of almost every match. subscribeToNewRoom (dispatch.go, INC-0012) correctly subscribes the room the moment match_found arrives, but the very next refreshRooms tick saw that same room missing from ListMyRooms's kept-only answer and treated it as the client having left, unsubscribing it - with no error, since from refreshRooms's perspective this looked like an entirely ordinary room departure, the same path a real room_left would take.
resolution: refreshRooms now folds currentMatchRoomID (the one piece of connection state that already tracks the active, possibly-still-undecided match room - set by trackMatchRoom on match_found, cleared on match_ended) into its view of "current" rooms before computing what to unsubscribe, so an active match's room is never dropped just because it hasn't been kept yet. Verified with a new integration test (TestRefreshRoomsDoesNotUnsubscribeAnUndecidedMatch) that constructs a connection with an empty ListMyRooms response (mirroring the real undecided-match case exactly) and asserts the room's real Redis subscriber count stays at 1 after refreshRooms runs - confirmed to fail against the old code (0 subscribers) and pass against the fix. Re-verified live: a real two-browser random match, messages sent both immediately after match and again more than 30 seconds later (crossing the real 25-second tick), all delivered to both sides.
lessons: The same precise distinction INC-0012 already drew - a live event with a hook to react to (match_found) versus state that has to be polled (a room joined over HTTP) - needed to be drawn a second time here, in the opposite direction: refreshRooms's periodic poll is correct for picking up rooms this connection doesn't yet know about, but was never safe to treat as the sole source of truth for which rooms to keep, since the thing it polls (ListMyRooms) has its own, unrelated reason to omit an undecided match. A unit or integration test that only checks "does subscribing work" (INC-0012's own regression test) does not catch a later step silently undoing it - this needed a test that let real time-shaped logic (refreshRooms's diff against a stale-by-design list) run against the exact state it would see in production, not just the happy path immediately after a match.

title: A random match's chat gets a 30-second grace window to keep it solo after the partner leaves, instead of vanishing instantly
context: v1 scope (DEC-0031, PRD's History section) says a random 1:1 chat disappears for both sides when it ends unless both voted keep_chat first - in practice this meant: the instant either side clicked End/Next, the other side's screen snapped back to "Find a match" with no warning and no way to save the conversation, even one message after a match. The maintainer tried this live and found it jarring and wanted a choice offered instead of a silent vanish.
options: Let the remaining person keep the chat unconditionally, any time after the partner leaves
Only improve the transition (show "your partner left" before returning to Find a match) but keep the hard rule that keeping requires both sides present
Give the remaining person a short grace window after the partner leaves during which their own vote is enough on its own to keep it
decision: match_ended now tells the client who ended it (RoomEnded.ended_by_account_id, threaded through from EndDirectRoomRequest - mirroring MatchEnded's existing account_id/you_left/partner_left framing, which the explicit End-button path didn't have before this). When the partner leaves, the frontend shows a "Your partner left this chat - keep it anyway?" prompt with a 30-second countdown instead of dropping the match immediately. chat's VoteKeep (services/chat/internal/store) accepts a solo vote within store.VoteKeepGraceWindow (30s) of the room ending as sufficient to mark it kept, since the side that left can never complete a mutual vote at that point.
rationale: Requiring both sides present to keep a chat makes sense while the conversation is live, but becomes a trap the instant one side leaves - the remaining person's intent to keep it can never be completed under the old rule, through no fault of their own. A time-boxed solo vote preserves the spirit of "keeping is a deliberate choice" (not automatic, not retroactive from arbitrarily long ago) while actually leaving that choice open to the person still there.
tradeoffs: The grace window's length (30s) is a guess, not measured against real usage - may need tuning once real users hit it. The window is enforced server-side (not just cosmetically in the UI) so it can't be gamed by a stale client, but someone who steps away from their screen for longer than 30 seconds after their partner leaves still loses the option, same shape of problem as before just with a longer fuse. Two related gaps found while building this were deliberately left out of this change: closing the tab (rather than clicking End/Next) still doesn't notify the partner at all today, and reloading mid-match still loses the client's way back into an active, undecided chat - both need their own timer/heartbeat-based design, not a bolt-on here.

title: Google sign-in moves to gateway's own server-side OAuth redirect flow, off the in-page widget
context: The in-page Google Identity Services widget (built for T11) requires Google to trust the exact page origin it renders on - which means whatever free host serves the web UI (Vercel, Render, a student-pack domain) would need its own Google brand verification: a owned, DNS-verified domain, a privacy policy, and (per DEC-0033) the maintainer specifically did not want a personal domain tied to the app's own address. The maintainer does not currently have budget for a dedicated project domain, but does own a personal domain (aranyadutta.dev) they were willing to use for a piece of infrastructure that never appears in the app's own address - following the same pattern a real hosted auth provider (Clerk, observed directly: a hobby app on a free Render subdomain signs in through Clerk's own already-verified Google OAuth client, with the consent screen showing "Clerk" rather than that app's name) uses for its own free tier.
options: Buy or claim a free project domain (GitHub Student Pack) and host the whole app there, satisfying Google's requirement directly (DEC-0033's original plan)
Use a third-party auth provider (Clerk) and accept its branding on the Google consent screen in exchange for zero domain/verification work

Build a self-built identity provider, scoped to Flamingo only: one small page on a domain the maintainer already owns (auth.aranyadutta.dev) that does the actual Google OAuth exchange via a real server-side authorization-code flow, with the main app staying on any free host and redirecting out to it and back
decision: Gateway now implements the server-side half of Google's OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow itself: GET /v1/auth/google/start redirects the browser to Google (building the URL with the same COLLEGE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID identity already verifies ID token audiences against) and stashes a one-time CSRF state value in Redis; GET /v1/auth/google/callback exchanges the code Google returns for an ID token (services/gateway/internal/googleauth.Exchanger, a real HTTP client against Google's token endpoint) and completes the exact same sign-in path the old in-page flow used (identity.SignInWithGoogle, unchanged), then redirects the browser back to the frontend with the new session in the URL fragment (never sent to any server, unlike a query param). auth.aranyadutta.dev is the one domain that needs Google's brand verification; the actual web UI can stay on any free host. A DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE-gated bypass (mirroring identity's own DEC-0049) skips the real Google hop entirely in local development, so the whole round trip is testable without real credentials. The old POST /v1/auth/google endpoint (a client-supplied ID token, no redirect) is kept, not removed - tests/e2e still uses it to sign in as a verified user without driving a real browser.
rationale: This gets the same practical outcome a provider like Clerk's free tier gives (no domain cost, no brand-verification work on the app's own address) without the trade a shared/borrowed OAuth identity requires (the consent screen showing a third party's name, a real dependency on an external service for the single most security-critical path in the app) and without the larger, premature scope of building a reusable multi-app identity platform the maintainer doesn't have a second app to justify yet. Keeping the work scoped to Flamingo - a real server-side OAuth flow for one app, not a general auth provider - matches the project's own stated secondary goal of learning this kind of infrastructure hands-on, which outsourcing to Clerk would have skipped entirely.
tradeoffs: More code to build and maintain than either alternative (a real redirect flow, a CSRF-protected state store, a token-exchange client) - verified end to end locally (unit tests, integration tests against real Redis via the dev-fake path, and a live two-browser run: both fresh sign-in and guest-to-verified upgrade), but the real Google exchange itself is still unverified against the actual Google OAuth client, pending the maintainer completing auth.aranyadutta.dev's domain verification and OAuth consent screen configuration - that is tracked as separate, maintainer-owned follow-up work, not blocking this PR.

title: Prometheus metrics (/metrics on every service, a request-duration histogram in pkg/grpclog) - T12, vendor-neutral by design
context: T12 of the build plan calls for observability hooks in code, if time allows: /metrics on every service, request metrics in pkg/grpclog, consumer lag metrics, and trace context through gRPC and Kafka. The maintainer has not yet decided which monitoring stack to run this against (a dedicated discussion was deferred on purpose) - this work needed to not presuppose that choice.
options: Wait until the monitoring stack is chosen before writing any instrumentation code

Instrument with a vendor-neutral, de facto standard (Prometheus's client library) that works unmodified regardless of which stack eventually scrapes it - self-hosted Prometheus, or a managed service that speaks the same exposition format
decision: Added github.com/prometheus/client_golang (v1.25.0) to pkg, used in two places: a new pkg/metrics.Serve(addr, logger) started as its own goroutine (go metrics.Serve(":"+metricsPort, logger)) in every service's main.go, including the two Kafka-only workers that have no server of their own otherwise; and pkg/grpclog's existing unary interceptor, which now records a Prometheus histogram (grpc_server_request_duration_seconds, labeled by method and status code) alongside the structured log line it already wrote per request. The default Prometheus registry already includes Go runtime and process collectors for free, so even a worker with no custom metric yet exposes goroutine/GC/CPU/memory data. The Helm chart's shared values.yaml gained a metricsPort default (9090), with the Deployment template declaring that container port unconditionally (workers included) and the Service template exposing it alongside the main protocol port for services that have one.
rationale: Prometheus's exposition format is the one instrumentation choice that doesn't lock in a backend - self-hosted Prometheus/Grafana and GCP's own Managed Service for Prometheus both scrape the exact same /metrics output, so this work is valid regardless of which way the pending monitoring-stack discussion goes. pkg/grpclog was the obvious place for the request-duration histogram specifically because its own doc comment already said as much, written when the interceptor was first built.
tradeoffs: Distributed tracing (the other half of T12) was deliberately left out of this pass - unlike metrics, a trace needs a configured exporter/backend to be worth anything at all, which is exactly the choice still pending; wiring OpenTelemetry now would mean guessing at that choice instead of waiting for it. Consumer lag metrics for delivery-worker/persistence-worker were also left out - both already expose /metrics and the default collectors, but a real per-partition lag gauge needs its own small design pass (periodic polling of sarama's client against each partition's high watermark), not a one-line addition like the rest of this change.

title: Consumer lag metric for delivery-worker and persistence-worker, derived from each message's own claim instead of a separate poller
context: DEC-0093 (T12's Prometheus pass) deliberately left consumer lag out, noting it would need its own small design pass rather than a one-line addition - the obvious approach (periodically poll each partition's high water mark with a separate sarama client) adds a second connection and a polling loop to each worker just to read a number sarama already hands the consumer on every message.
options: Add a periodic poller: a second sarama client per worker that calls GetOffset against each partition's latest offset on a timer, independent of message flow
Read sarama.ConsumerGroupClaim.HighWaterMarkOffset() - already passed into ConsumeClaim for every claim - at the point each message is handled, with no extra client or goroutine
decision: Both services/delivery-worker/internal/consumer/handler.go and services/persistence-worker/internal/consumer/handler.go now thread the claim through from ConsumeClaim into handle, and record a kafka_consumer_lag gauge (labeled topic, partition) via a new recordLag(claim, msg) call at the top of handle: lag = claim.HighWaterMarkOffset() - msg.Offset - 1, clamped to 0. HighWaterMarkOffset is sarama's own words for "the offset that will be used for the next message that will be produced", so this is the count of messages still waiting on that partition as of the message just received.
rationale: The high water mark is already available on the exact object ConsumeClaim receives per message - no new client, connection, or background goroutine is needed, and the gauge updates on real message flow rather than a fixed timer. Label cardinality stays bounded because partition count is small and fixed per topic (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md's Kafka topics).
tradeoffs: The gauge only updates when a message is actually consumed, so a partition that goes fully idle (no new messages at all) freezes its last-known lag value rather than reflecting a growing backlog from producers the consumer hasn't caught up to - a periodic poller wouldn't have this gap. Accepted: both workers' topics see steady traffic in practice, and closing this gap later (if it matters) is additive, not a rework of this change.

title: Self-hosted Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Alloy for dev-cluster observability, distributed tracing deferred
context: PLAN.md's 'Monitoring design (the stack and dashboards)' had been deliberately left open while T12 (DEC-0093, DEC-0094) built vendor-neutral metrics instrumentation without presupposing a backend. The maintainer asked which stack to actually run that instrumentation against, and separately whether to stand up logs/dashboards before the already-planned load test rather than after.
options: GCP-managed observability (Managed Service for Prometheus, Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace) once the GCP cluster exists
A commercial SaaS (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana Cloud free tier)
Self-hosted, Kubernetes-native OSS (Prometheus + Grafana for metrics, Loki + Alloy for logs), deployed the same way everything else in deploy/ is - a Helm release per component, dev-scoped values
decision: Installed prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack (chart 92.10.1: Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, kube-state-metrics, node-exporter, all at single-replica/no-PVC dev scale) and grafana/loki (chart 7.3.0, SingleBinary deployment mode, filesystem storage - not the chart's SimpleScalable default, which is sized for real production volume) plus grafana/alloy (chart 1.14.0, DaemonSet, replacing the now-EOL Promtail) as the log shipper, all under deploy/observability/ with pinned chart versions and dev-only values. Every service's shared Helm chart (deploy/helm/service) gained a PodMonitor template, gated behind a podMonitor.enabled flag (default off, so it's a no-op anywhere the CRD isn't installed) - a PodMonitor rather than a ServiceMonitor because it scrapes pods by label directly, which also covers delivery-worker/persistence-worker, which have no Service object at all (DEC-0066). Tiltfile now installs the three observability releases via local_resource (Tilt's own helm() function only handles local chart directories, not repo-hosted ones) and passes podMonitor.enabled=true when deploying every service. Live-verified end to end: Prometheus actually scraping delivery-worker/persistence-worker's real /metrics (confirmed via Prometheus's own /api/v1/query, not just curling /metrics directly), and a real delivery-worker log line observed in Loki with correct labels, both reached through Alloy with zero application-code changes. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry + Tempo) is explicitly deferred - no cross-service latency problem exists yet to debug, and propagating trace context across Kafka message headers (not just gRPC metadata) is nontrivial, unbuilt work this project doesn't have a concrete need for yet.
rationale: The project has a hard deadline to migrate off Google Cloud (DEC-0023, by 2026-12-25's trial expiry) - building observability against GCP-managed services now would mean rebuilding it from scratch within two months. Kubernetes-native self-hosted OSS is the only option that survives that move unchanged, since it is just another workload in whatever cluster the app runs on next. A SaaS was ruled out for the same cost-sensitivity that already drove DEC-0092's authentication redesign, and because self-hosting this stack is itself part of the project's stated distributed-systems learning goal (AGENTS.md), not a detour from it. Loki over the ELK stack specifically because it is far lighter at this traffic scale and shares Prometheus's label model, letting Grafana pivot between a metric and its matching logs natively. Alloy over Promtail because Promtail is actually past end-of-life (2026-03-02); Alloy is Grafana's current, OpenTelemetry-Collector-based replacement, and since it is already in place for logs, it is also the natural place to carry trace data later without introducing a third agent.
tradeoffs: This is dev-cluster scope only - production hosting (self-hosted again vs. a managed service, real retention and storage, HA) is explicitly not decided here and depends on where the app actually runs once it migrates off GCP. kube-prometheus-stack's defaults (10d Prometheus retention, 10Gi Loki PVC) were scaled down for a disposable single-node kind cluster and would need revisiting for anything longer-lived. No custom per-service Grafana dashboards exist yet - only the chart's own default cluster dashboards; building dashboards that actually reflect this app's own metrics is follow-up work. Tracing's deferral means a genuine cross-service latency investigation today still has to be done by hand from per-service metrics and logs alone.

title: Every service image build hung forever after a Docker Desktop restart, blocking tilt up for most of a day
what_happened: From 2026-10-20 01:56 UTC, when Docker Desktop restarted after its WSL integration dropped mid-build, every build of a service image ran every step, saved the image, and then never returned - not from Tilt, not from a plain docker build. Tilt only tags an image, loads it into kind and deploys after the build call returns, so every Go service sat at pending/in_progress indefinitely. BuildKit's own history showed 26 builds still 'Running', the oldest 16 hours old, including builds whose clients had been killed. Small test builds kept completing normally, which is why this hid behind earlier 'Tilt is flaky' diagnoses for most of the session.
impact: No service could be built or redeployed locally for roughly 17 hours. Several hours went into workarounds (bypassing Tilt with manual docker build + kind load) and wrong diagnoses before the cause was found.
root_cause: Bisected with about twenty probe builds down to a two-line Dockerfile - FROM golang:1.27.2-bookworm, WORKDIR /src - that hung only when that WORKDIR step came from BuildKit's cache (the log labelled it [build 2/5], i.e. it was reused from one of our own service builds); the same lines with any other directory completed in seconds. Ruled out along the way, each by a passing probe: the daemon being globally wedged, cache mounts (read or write), a git build context, the dockerfile:1 syntax frontend, the build-context path, file count, using -f, and each base image on its own. The likely origin is the build cut off by the 01:56 restart leaving that cache entry broken; one copy was deletable, but a second stayed locked (Reclaimable: false), most likely by the stuck builds. Also unrelated, but seen while investigating: dockerd logs a failed OpenTelemetry trace export every 5 seconds, going back to at least 2026-10-17 when builds still worked - noise, not the cause. The exact BuildKit-internal mechanism was not proven.
resolution: Fully quit and restarted Docker Desktop (clearing the stuck builds and their locks), then docker builder prune -af, confirmed with the two-line build completing. That restart in turn left the kind node stopped: Docker's single retry of its on-failure:1 restart policy was OOM-killed at container init, so Tilt's Helm steps failed with 'cluster unreachable' until the node was started again with docker start flamingo-dev-control-plane.
lessons: When a build looks hung, check docker buildx history ls before blaming Tilt: a pile of 'Running' builds means the daemon, not the client, is stuck. Verify a build hang by looking for the image (docker images) and the history record, not the client's exit. After restarting Docker Desktop, check that the kind node actually came back (docker ps -a). The whole local stack shares one 7.6 GB WSL VM; the kind node being OOM-killed on restart is a warning that memory is close to its limit with the observability stack added.

title: A Tiltfile change deleted six services' PodMonitors under a running tilt up, and stale Prometheus values hid it
what_happened: Changing the Tiltfile to attach each service's PodMonitor to that service (objects=['<name>:podmonitor']) instead of Tilt's 'uncategorized' bucket was picked up live by an already-running tilt up. Tilt removed the PodMonitors from 'uncategorized', which deletes them, and only re-created the two whose resources it redeployed afterwards (the workers). Prometheus' config reload at 19:11:48 dropped six scrape jobs. Queries kept returning values for several minutes afterwards, because Prometheus returns a series' last sample for up to 5 minutes after it stops - so the first checks reported 'working' when nothing had been scraped since the reload.
impact: Prometheus stopped scraping gateway, identity, chat, matching, presence and moderation for about five minutes, and the new dashboard's request panels looked mysteriously empty until the cause was found.
root_cause: Tilt deletes objects that a Tiltfile reload moves out of a resource, and re-applies them under the new resource only when that resource next updates. Separately, request-rate panels stay empty after a single short burst of traffic even when scraping works: a counter series only comes into existence on its first request, so Prometheus' first sample of it already holds the final value and rate() has no increase to measure - confirmed when a second e2e run filled every panel.
resolution: tilt trigger on the six affected services re-applied their PodMonitors; all eight targets were scraped again within a minute. A fresh tilt up creates every PodMonitor normally, so this only bites when the change lands under a running Tilt.
lessons: Check timestamp(up{...}) or Prometheus' targets page, not a current-value query, to prove a service is being scraped right now. After moving k8s objects between Tilt resources, trigger the receiving resources or restart tilt up. Pre-initialising each method's counter at zero when a gRPC server starts would make even the first burst of traffic visible - not done yet.

title: Dashboards as code, provisioned through Grafana's sidecar, and Tilt-managed links for the observability UIs
context: After DEC-0095 the monitoring stack ran but was hard to reach: Tilt showed no links for the web app or any observability UI (the Helm releases are created by local_resource shell commands, which Tilt doesn't track), and Grafana had only the chart's generic Kubernetes dashboards, nothing about Flamingo's own services.
options: Build dashboards by hand in Grafana's UI and keep them only in its database
Embed dashboard JSON in kube-prometheus-stack's Helm values
Keep each dashboard as a plain JSON file in the repo and turn the folder into a ConfigMap Grafana's sidecar loads automatically
decision: deploy/observability/dashboards/ holds one JSON file per dashboard; the Tiltfile turns that folder into a ConfigMap labelled grafana_dashboard=1 (generated with kubectl create configmap --dry-run, watched with watch_file), which kube-prometheus-stack's Grafana sidecar picks up from any namespace. The first dashboard, Flamingo overview, covers service health, gRPC request rate, errors by code and p95 latency per method (health checks excluded), Kafka consumer lag per worker/topic/partition, goroutines, memory and a Loki logs panel with health-check lines filtered out. It picks its Prometheus and Loki datasources through dashboard variables instead of hard-coded datasource UIDs, since Loki's UID is generated. The Tiltfile also gains links for the web app and three port-forward resources (Grafana, Prometheus, Alloy's UI) running kubectl port-forward in a retry loop, with Grafana's generated admin password printed to its Tilt log rather than committed; .dockerignore now excludes the Tiltfile so editing it no longer rebuilds every service image.
rationale: A dashboard that exists only in Grafana's database is lost whenever the dev cluster is rebuilt, and is invisible in code review. A JSON file per dashboard can be exported from Grafana's UI after editing and diffed in a pull request, without wrapping it in Helm values. Datasource variables keep the same file usable against any Grafana, including whatever production ends up running.
tradeoffs: Edits made in Grafana's UI are not saved back automatically - they have to be exported to the JSON file by hand.
