Gateway is HTTP, so it has no request metrics of its own on this dashboard; its calls only show on the gRPC services behind it. The port-forward resources are a workaround for Tilt not tracking Helm-created Services, and the loki/alloy Tilt resources still re-download their charts from GitHub on every tilt up, which failed repeatedly today on this network even though both were already installed.

title: Grafana kept getting OOM-killed and the monitoring stack looked broken because its resource values were guessed, not measured
what_happened: Opening Grafana showed "If you're seeing this Grafana has failed to load its application files", and Prometheus' Target health page showed only one entry. Investigation found four separate problems. Grafana's memory limit (256Mi, set in DEC-0095's values without measuring) was exactly its working set: kube-state-metrics recorded OOMKilled restarts, so the process died mid page-load and the browser got only some of its JavaScript. Prometheus peaked at 385Mi of its 512Mi limit. Alloy's resources had been put at the top level of its values file, which that chart ignores, leaving it with no limit at all. Four control-plane targets (controller-manager, scheduler, etcd, kube-proxy) were permanently down, firing four TargetDown alerts and an etcdInsufficientMembers alert. Separately, Prometheus' own UI hides all but the first scrape pool once there are more than 20 (its code: 'There are more than 20 scrape pools. Showing only the first one.'), and the stack has 21 to 25, which is why only one entry appeared - not a fault.
impact: Grafana unusable intermittently; false alerts; a misleading Target health page; a missing memory limit that would only have been noticed under pressure.
root_cause: Resource limits in deploy/observability were written as plausible-looking guesses rather than sized from measurement, and one setting was placed under the wrong key without rendering the chart to check it. The control-plane targets are unreachable on kind by design: those components only listen on the node's own 127.0.0.1.
resolution: Sized from a day of real usage pulled from Prometheus (max_over_time of container_memory_working_set_bytes): Grafana 384Mi request / 768Mi limit (it sits near 380Mi uncapped), Prometheus 384Mi / 1Gi, Alloy 128Mi / 256Mi under the alloy: key the chart reads. Disabled kubeControllerManager, kubeScheduler, kubeEtcd and kubeProxy in the dev values, which also drops their alert rules. Verified by rendering both charts from Helm's cache, then live: all three pods on the new limits with no restarts, every Prometheus target up, and all of Grafana's application files loading. README now explains the 20-pool banner and that the query `up` lists every target.
lessons: Measure before setting a limit; Prometheus already has the data (container_memory_working_set_bytes, kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason). Render a chart with the new values (helm template) to prove a setting lands where intended before deploying it. A Grafana 'failed to load application files' page is often the server dying mid-load rather than a configuration problem.

title: Root cause of INC-0015's hanging image builds: a BuildKit bug in Docker Engine 28.4.0, triggered by cache from before a Docker restart
what_happened: The build hang from INC-0015 came back on 2026-10-21 after Docker restarted at 05:36 UTC (every service build finished its steps, saved nothing and never returned; BuildKit history showed them 'Running'). INC-0015's cleanup had only been a temporary fix.
impact: No images could be built or deployed for a second time in two days, blocking verification of the gateway HTTP metrics and gRPC counter work (DEC-0098).
root_cause: Confirmed with paired probes: a build that reuses a cache entry created before the most recent Docker daemon restart hangs (FROM golang + WORKDIR /src, CACHED, never returned), while a build that reuses an entry created after the restart completes in six seconds. That matches moby/buildkit issue #6209 ('Image export to local store via buildx hangs indefinitely': the client hangs after the build reports DONE and later builds are affected too), reported on BuildKit v0.24.0 - the version this Docker Desktop 4.47.0 / Engine 28.4.0 runs. Its fixes, including moby/buildkit PR #6186 ('solver: Resolve infinite loop when record is ErrNotFound'), shipped in Docker Engine 28.5.0, where the reporter saw no further occurrences. INC-0015's 'one corrupted cache entry' theory was incomplete: any pre-restart cache entry triggers it, which is why pruning after a restart fixed it until the next restart.
resolution: Pending: update Docker Desktop (4.47.0 is far behind; the release notes list 4.86.0, 2026-08-10, and any version bundling Engine 28.5.0 or later contains the fix), then run docker builder prune -af once and confirm a build that reuses cache completes. Until then the workaround is INC-0015's: restart Docker Desktop, docker builder prune -af, rebuild.
lessons: When a workaround only holds until the next restart, the diagnosis is not finished. Check the tool's version against its upstream issue tracker early - this was a known, fixed bug in a year-old Docker Desktop.

title: Observability Helm releases are installed only when their chart version or values change
context: The Tiltfile ran helm upgrade --install <repo/chart> for kube-prometheus-stack, Loki and Alloy on every tilt up. Helm re-downloads a repo chart each time even when its archive is already in the local cache, so whenever GitHub's release-asset host was slow from this network the step failed and Tilt showed Loki (and Alloy, which waits on it) red, even though both were installed and healthy.
options: Keep reinstalling on every tilt up and live with network failures
Vendor the chart archives into the repository
Skip the install when the deployed release already matches, and install from Helm's local chart cache when the version is already there
decision: deploy/observability/ensure-release.sh fingerprints chart reference, version and values file (sha256), compares it with the fingerprint stored after the last successful install (ConfigMap tilt-helm-releases), and does nothing when the release is deployed at that chart version with the same fingerprint. Otherwise it installs from Helm's local cache (helm pull first only if that version isn't cached) and records the new fingerprint. The Tiltfile calls it per release with the values file and the script as deps, so editing a values file re-applies it while tilt up runs, and a failed helm repo update is now a warning rather than an error.
rationale: Makes tilt up independent of the network whenever nothing changed (verified: three releases checked in 6 seconds, versus several minutes of re-downloads and --wait), while a values change still triggers exactly one upgrade (verified with the Grafana memory change). Vendoring archives would add binary blobs to the repository for a dev-only concern.
tradeoffs: A change made to a release outside this script (a manual helm upgrade) won't be noticed, because the stored fingerprint still matches - delete the ConfigMap entry or edit the values file to force a reinstall. The script lives under deploy/observability rather than scripts/ so editing it doesn't trigger image rebuilds (deploy/ is in .dockerignore).

title: Gateway records HTTP request metrics by route pattern, and gRPC services start every request counter at zero
context: Gateway serves HTTP, so it had no request metrics at all - its traffic only showed up indirectly on the gRPC services behind it. And the dashboard's request-rate panels stayed empty after a single burst of traffic, because a counter series only came into existence on its first request: Prometheus' first sample already held the final value, leaving rate() nothing to measure (INC-0016).
options: Label HTTP metrics by raw URL path
Label them by the matched route pattern
For the empty panels: accept it, or pre-create every known series at zero at startup
decision: services/gateway/internal/httpapi.Metrics wraps the ServeMux directly (inside CORS) and records http_server_request_duration_seconds{route, code}, where route is the pattern the mux matched (r.Pattern, e.g. 'GET /v1/rooms/{id}/messages') and every unknown path is 'unmatched'. A hijacked connection - a WebSocket upgrade - is passed through untouched and not recorded, since its duration is a whole session. pkg/grpclog.InitializeMetrics creates every unary method's series at zero (code OK) from the server's own registry; each gRPC service calls it after registering its services. The dashboard gained a Gateway (HTTP) row, with Kubernetes' /healthz and /readyz probes excluded.
rationale: Labelling by pattern keeps the number of series fixed no matter how many rooms or users exist, and stops scanners from creating a series per probed URL - unbounded label values (cardinality) are the classic way to make Prometheus run out of memory. Pre-creating series at zero is Prometheus' own recommended practice for known label combinations, and the gRPC server already knows every method it serves.
tradeoffs: Only code=OK is pre-created, so the first occurrence of an error code after a restart still needs a second occurrence to show as a rate; gateway's HTTP series are not pre-created at all (the status codes a route can return aren't known up front), so its panels need traffic on two scrapes. WebSocket activity has no metric yet - an active-connections gauge would be the natural next one.

title: CI's vulncheck started failing on every service after a Go standard-library vulnerability (GO-2026-6809) was published
what_happened: PR #30's vulncheck job failed for all eight services, including two the PR didn't touch. govulncheck reported GO-2026-6809 in crypto/x509, found in go1.27.2 and fixed in go1.27.3, reachable from our code (gateway: ratelimit.init calls redis.NewScript, which eventually calls x509.Certificate.Verify). The same check had passed the day before: the vulnerability was published in between, so main was affected too.
impact: Every pull request blocked by a required check until the Go version moved.
root_cause: A new advisory against the pinned Go patch release; nothing in the code changed.
resolution: CI's GO_VERSION and every service Dockerfile's build image moved to 1.27.3 (go1.27.3 is the current release on go.dev; golang:1.27.3-bookworm was published to Docker Hub on 2026-10-21), so CI scans and the images ship the fixed standard library. Unlike DEC-0051, the `go` line in every go.mod and go.work stays at 1.27.2: it is the minimum version, and with GOTOOLCHAIN=local raising it would make every local build fail until that machine's Go is upgraded, which a stdlib-only fix doesn't require. AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md now describe the minimum-versus-build-version split.
lessons: A vulncheck failure across modules a change didn't touch points at a newly published advisory, not the change. Keeping the go directive as a minimum and pinning the build toolchain separately lets patch releases move without forcing every contributor to upgrade at once.

title: Pilot deployment: one zonal GKE Standard node behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, images from GHCR, data stores in the cluster
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §12 left the deployment undesigned (cluster mode and region, node size and verified cost, Postgres and Kafka on the cluster, monitoring, pipeline, Cloudflare's role). The maintainer wants a closed beta live on 2026-10-21. Google caps OAuth sign-in at 100 users until the app is verified, so this is a closed beta, not the public launch.
options: GKE Autopilot
GKE Standard, zonal, one e2-standard-2 node
Spot nodes
A Google load balancer with cert-manager for HTTPS
A Cloudflare Tunnel
Artifact Registry
GitHub Container Registry
decision: Accepted by the maintainer on 2026-10-21 (D1-D7 as proposed): GKE Standard, zonal (asia-south1-a), one e2-standard-2 node with a 50 GB standard boot disk, Google's managed Prometheus off and only system logging/monitoring (deploy/gke/create-cluster.sh); Postgres and Kafka as StatefulSets on persistent disks and Redis in memory (deploy/k8s/prod/); a Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared, two replicas) as the only way in, so nothing has a public IP and gateway trusts CF-Connecting-IP for the client address; gateway at auth.aranyadutta.dev (DEC-0092) and the web app on Vercel's own subdomain (DEC-0032/0033); images built by GitHub Actions on merge to main and pushed to GHCR, deployed only deliberately with deploy/prod/deploy.sh <sha>; production overlays (deploy/helm/service/values/prod/, deploy/observability/prod/) that remove every dev-only setting, with secrets in Kubernetes Secrets created by deploy/prod/create-secrets.sh; Turnstile left off for the beta.
rationale: Priced from Google's Cloud Billing Catalog API on 2026-10-21 for asia-south1: e2 at $0.026199 per vCPU-hour and $0.003511 per GiB-hour, so the node is about $58.75 a month; the cluster fee is covered by the free tier ('One free Autopilot or zonal Standard cluster per month', cluster charge only); balanced disk $0.12 and standard disk $0.048 per GiB-month; internet egress to India $0.12 per GiB. Total about $70 a month, about $128 until the 2026-12-15 move-off. A load balancer would add a $0.025-$0.030 per hour forwarding-rule minimum plus a static IP; the tunnel avoids that and opens no ports, and WebSockets work through it (Cloudflare's FAQ: 'Cloudflare Tunnel has full support for Websockets'). Autopilot costs about the same but restricts host access, which breaks node-exporter; Spot nodes can be preempted, and with one node that is an outage. GHCR is free for public images (GitHub's billing docs). Sizing: on the dev cluster, sum(container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!="",container!="POD"}) was 2.83 GiB at 2026-10-21T13:31Z, and max_over_time of that sum over the previous 24 hours (1-minute steps) was 5.16 GiB - a window that included rolling restarts and an extra test Postgres and Kafka. An e2-standard-2 has 8 GiB, part of it reserved by GKE; the exact allocatable memory is to be read from the real node.
tradeoffs: One node is a single point of failure: a node upgrade (window 03:00-07:00 IST) or failure takes the whole app down for minutes. Kafka has no replication. Cloudflare Tunnel's price was not found stated on an official Cloudflare page. GHCR packages start private and must each be made public once by hand. Turnstile stays off until the web app has the widget, so guest signup is protected only by the per-IP rate limit. Message retention (D8, decided the same day): the closed-beta privacy notice states plainly that messages are stored, including random chats that disappear from the screen; deleting un-kept chats after a set time comes before the public launch.

title: Kafka's image silently hid its persistent disk: every restart would have wiped all topics and events
what_happened: Testing the production Kafka StatefulSet in a throwaway namespace on kind, a topic created before deleting the pod was gone afterwards, even though a marker file on the same disk survived. Kafka's storage ID changed and its metadata log shrank from 23,698 to 3,374 bytes: the storage had been freshly formatted at startup.
impact: Caught before production. Had it shipped, every Kafka restart (node upgrade, crash, reschedule) would have lost every topic and every event not yet consumed. The dev cluster has the same mount, unnoticed because dev storage is throwaway anyway.
root_cause: Kafka's official Dockerfile declares VOLUME ["/etc/kafka/secrets", "/var/lib/kafka/data", "/mnt/shared/config"]. The container runtime gives every new container a fresh, empty mount at /var/lib/kafka/data, layered over the persistent disk mounted one level up at /var/lib/kafka (the pod's /proc/mounts showed both). Kafka found empty storage and formatted it on every start; the image's format step itself correctly refuses already-formatted storage. Separately, without KAFKA_LOG_DIRS this image writes to /tmp/kafka-logs, not to any mounted volume at all.
resolution: deploy/k8s/prod/kafka.yaml mounts the disk exactly at /var/lib/kafka/data, replacing the image's throwaway mount, with KAFKA_LOG_DIRS=/var/lib/kafka/data/logs (a subdirectory, since a fresh cloud disk contains lost+found). Verified: storage ID unchanged across a pod restart, the topic survived, and a message produced before the restart was read back after it.
lessons: Prove persistence by restarting the pod and reading data back, not by checking that a volume is bound. Read an image's Dockerfile for VOLUME declarations before mounting storage near those paths.

title: Two ways a production config could have shipped with fake Google sign-in or without its secrets
what_happened: Preparing the production overlays turned up two traps. Gateway and identity enabled DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE for any non-empty value, so a value of "0" or "false" - which reads as off - would have accepted fabricated sign-ins as any verified student. And setting a key to null in an overlay does not remove it: the rendered manifests still contained DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE, SESSION_SIGNING_KEY, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET and POSTGRES_URL as empty env vars, and an explicit env var overrides the same name coming from a Secret.
impact: Caught before any production deploy. Shipped as written, gateway would not have started (empty signing key), services would have pointed at a database address that doesn't exist, and a well-meant DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE="0" would have opened account impersonation.
root_cause: The flag was parsed as 'set means on'. Helm drops nulls only when they override the chart's own defaults, not between user-supplied values files.
resolution: Both services now accept only exactly "1". The service chart's Deployment and CronJob templates skip env entries whose value is null, so an overlay's null really removes a variable, and the CronJob gained envFromSecret (without it identity's guest-cleanup job would have lost POSTGRES_URL). deploy/prod/check-render.py refuses any production render containing DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE, an empty env var, a secret in a plain env var, the CHANGE-ME placeholder or a non-GHCR image, and deploy/prod/deploy.sh runs it before changing anything.
lessons: Check what a template actually renders rather than what the values file says. A boolean switch should have one exact 'on' value. Guard production deploys with an automated check of the rendered output.

title: Start Google brand verification before the deploy: a static homepage, privacy notice and terms at accounts.aranyadutta.dev, and Google's own sign-in button
context: Google's brand verification is what shows the app's name on the consent screen, and has to be done before a public launch. It needs a public homepage that describes the app (not only a login page), a privacy policy on the same domain linked from it, the domain verified in Search Console, and sign-in buttons that follow Google's branding guidelines (developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification, support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321). None of that needs the cluster, and the automated check 'typically takes a few minutes' while a manual review 'usually takes 2-3 business days', so the maintainer asked to start it in parallel with the deploy.
options: Wait until the app is deployed and serve the pages from gateway
A page on the maintainer's existing personal site (aranyadutta.dev)
A separate static site on its own subdomain, from a folder in this repository, on Cloudflare Pages
decision: site/ holds three plain HTML pages (homepage, privacy notice, terms) and a stylesheet, with no build step, served by Cloudflare Pages at accounts.aranyadutta.dev, the host the maintainer chose. Every statement in the privacy notice was checked against the code on 2026-10-21, including what it would be easy to leave out: messages are kept even after a chat disappears from the screen (DEC-0099's D8), message text is also in the usage-event log, and other students' apps receive your random account ID. The web app's text link is replaced by Google's own pre-approved dark pill button image (signin-assets.zip), used unmodified, in a GoogleSignInLink component shared by the sign-in screen and the verify popover. site/ is in .dockerignore so editing it never rebuilds the service images.
rationale: A static site has no dependency on the cluster, Vercel or the tunnel, so verification can start today and doesn't block or get blocked by the deploy. A separate subdomain keeps it out of the personal site's repository while staying on a domain the maintainer owns. Google's own image is the surest way to pass the branding check, since the guidelines fix the logo, colours, padding and font.
tradeoffs: The privacy notice is a plain-language beta notice, not reviewed by a lawyer or against India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The pages must be kept in step with the code by hand; the retention section has to change when un-kept chats start being deleted. The contact address is the maintainer's own for now.

title: Rename the public hostnames before launch: flamingo-api.aranyadutta.dev for gateway, flamingo.aranyadutta.dev for the homepage
context: DEC-0092 named gateway's public address auth.aranyadutta.dev, because Google sign-in's callback was the reason it was needed, and DEC-0100 put the verification homepage at accounts.aranyadutta.dev. Once the deployment was laid out, both names described their job wrongly: auth.aranyadutta.dev carries all backend traffic (every API call and the WebSocket, not only sign-in), and accounts.aranyadutta.dev is Flamingo's homepage, privacy notice and terms, with nothing to do with accounts. The maintainer asked whether they could still change. Nothing depended on them yet: no deploy, no Vercel project, and the production redirect URI not yet registered with Google.
options: Keep auth.aranyadutta.dev and accounts.aranyadutta.dev
Generic first-level names: api.aranyadutta.dev and flamingo.aranyadutta.dev
Project-prefixed first-level names: flamingo-api.aranyadutta.dev and flamingo.aranyadutta.dev
Names nested under the project: api.flamingo.aranyadutta.dev and flamingo.aranyadutta.dev
decision: The maintainer moved both on 2026-10-24: the tunnel's published application is now flamingo-api.aranyadutta.dev -> http://gateway:8080 (Cloudflare created its DNS record), the Pages project serves flamingo.aranyadutta.dev, the Google Auth Platform branding URLs point at flamingo.aranyadutta.dev, and auth.aranyadutta.dev and accounts.aranyadutta.dev no longer resolve. In the repository, gateway's production GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI becomes https://flamingo-api.aranyadutta.dev/v1/auth/google/callback, and the comments and ARCHITECTURE §12 follow.
rationale: Each name now says what it is. The flamingo prefix leaves the rest of the personal domain free for other projects, where a bare api. would claim it for this one. Nesting under flamingo.aranyadutta.dev was ruled out because Cloudflare's free Universal SSL certificate covers only the apex and first-level subdomains: deeper names 'are not covered and will not serve a valid certificate' without the paid Advanced Certificate Manager or a custom certificate (developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/edge-certificates/universal-ssl/limitations/). Search Console verified the whole domain, so neither name needed new verification.
tradeoffs: Changing the branding URLs after Google's brand check creates a new draft that 'may need to go through the verification process again' and must be published within 7 days to keep verified status (support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549049). Both names are still on the maintainer's personal domain, which DEC-0033 wanted to avoid; a neutral project domain remains a later option. DEC-0092, DEC-0099 and DEC-0100 still name the old hosts; this entry replaces only their hostnames.

title: Keep the GHCR images private and let the cluster pull them with a read-only token, instead of making them public
context: DEC-0099 planned to make each of the eight ghcr.io/flamingo-apps packages public by hand so the cluster could pull them without a credential. On 2026-10-24 the maintainer could not change their visibility. The maintainer's GitHub account is a member, not an owner, of the Flamingo-Apps organization (GitHub API: role member); GitHub's docs leave a package's visibility to its admins and let an organization limit which visibility types members can use (docs.github.com/en/packages/learn-github-packages/configuring-a-packages-access-control-and-visibility). The maintainer also asked how companies handle this.
options: Make the packages public from the organization owner's account
Keep them private and give the cluster a pull credential: an image pull Secret built from a classic personal access token with only the read:packages scope
Mirror the images to Google Artifact Registry so the GKE nodes pull with their Google identity instead of a stored token
decision: Accepted by the maintainer on 2026-10-24 (option 2): keep the packages private. deploy/prod/create-secrets.sh creates a docker-registry Secret named ghcr-pull from a GitHub username and a classic personal access token with only read:packages (both asked for, the token hidden, if not set in the environment). The service chart gains an imagePullSecrets list, empty by default so dev is unchanged, and every values/prod/ overlay sets it to ghcr-pull, for the Deployment and identity's CronJob alike. deploy/prod/deploy.sh refuses to start without the Secret, and deploy/prod/check-render.py refuses a production pod that does not reference it.
rationale: A company's own images normally live in a private registry, and the cluster authenticates to pull them, with a cloud identity or a token Secret; public images are for software meant for others to run. This route works with the maintainer's own account today, without the organization owner. Each package carries the org.opencontainers.image.source label, so it is linked to this repository and 'inherits the access permissions (but not the visibility)' of it (GitHub docs, same page), which means a token from an account that can read the repository can pull. GitHub's billing docs say 'Container image storage and bandwidth for the Container registry is currently free', without distinguishing private from public images, and promise at least a month's notice before that changes (docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-packages). Artifact Registry would avoid a stored token, but adds a second registry and push step on a cloud the project leaves in December (DEC-0023).
tradeoffs: The token belongs to a person's account: it stops working if that account loses access to the repository, if it is revoked, or when it expires, and the failure only shows when a pod is next scheduled and cannot pull (ImagePullBackOff). A classic read:packages token can read every package that account can read, not only these. A dedicated machine account would remove the personal link; not worth it for the closed beta. The token's expiry date has to be tracked by hand.

title: Cluster creation stopped twice: re-linking an already-linked project failed with 'Cloud billing quota exceeded', then kubectl lacked GKE's auth plugin
what_happened: The first run of deploy/gke/create-cluster.sh for project flamingo-512316 stopped at `gcloud billing projects link` with FAILED_PRECONDITION 'Cloud billing quota exceeded' for billing account 017E36-2DAB86-661E91. The project had been created in the console and was already linked to that same account (billingEnabled true), alongside two other projects. The run was also reported as exit 0, because it was launched piped through grep without pipefail, so the failure was only visible in the output. The second run created the cluster, then failed at its last step, `kubectl get nodes`: kubectl authenticates to GKE through the gke-gcloud-auth-plugin executable, which was not installed. gcloud on this machine is the Windows Cloud SDK run by WSL's own Python with its config in ~/.config/gcloud, so neither the Windows SDK's components nor apt (sudo needs a password) were a clean way to add it.
impact: No cluster was created on the first run, which delayed the deploy until it was found. Nothing was changed on the account.
root_cause: The script linked billing unconditionally, assuming the call is a no-op for a project already on that account. It is not: the API applied the account's project quota to it. Google does not publish that quota ('Customers might have different quota', support.google.com/cloud/answer/6330231). The script also never checked that kubectl could reach GKE before creating anything.
resolution: The script now reads the project's current billing account and links only when it differs, as every other step already skips work that is done. The re-run passed the billing step and went on to create the cluster. The plugin was installed from Google's own apt package without root: the .deb for google-cloud-cli-gke-gcloud-auth-plugin 590.0.1 was downloaded from packages.cloud.google.com, its SHA256 checked against the repository's Packages index, and only the binary unpacked into ~/.local/bin; it reuses gcloud's existing login. The script now refuses to start when the plugin is missing.
lessons: An idempotent script needs every step checked, not only the ones that create something. Launch long scripts without a pipe, or with pipefail, so their exit code is the script's own. Check every tool a script needs before it spends money, not after.

title: First production deploy stopped: Kafka crash-looped because it could not write to its new Google persistent disk
what_happened: The first run of deploy/prod/deploy.sh brought up Postgres and Redis, then timed out after 5 minutes waiting for Kafka. kafka-0 was in CrashLoopBackOff, exiting with code 1 about 3 seconds after each start. Its log ended with 'Error while writing meta.properties file /var/lib/kafka/data/logs: java.nio.file.AccessDeniedException: /var/lib/kafka/data/logs'. A throwaway root pod mounting the same claim showed the disk's top directory as owner 0:0, mode 755, containing only lost+found.
impact: No user impact; nothing was public yet. The deploy script stopped at the data stores, as designed, so monitoring, the services and the tunnel were not installed until the fix.
root_cause: The apache/kafka image runs as appuser (uid and gid 1000) from the start, and a freshly formatted Google persistent disk (pd.csi.storage.gke.io, ext4) has a root-owned top directory that only root can write. The manifest set no pod securityContext. Postgres on the same kind of disk was unaffected because its image starts as root, fixes its data directory's ownership, then drops privileges. INC-0020's persistence test ran on kind, whose local-path volumes are writable by everyone, so the permission problem could not show there.
resolution: deploy/k8s/prod/kafka.yaml sets the pod securityContext to fsGroup 1000 with fsGroupChangePolicy OnRootMismatch, so Kubernetes gives the mounted disk to group 1000 before Kafka starts. The cluster's disk driver has fsGroupPolicy ReadWriteOnceWithFSType and the claims are ReadWriteOnce ext4, so the kubelet applies it. Checked with a server-side dry run before applying.
lessons: A storage test on kind proves the mount path, not the permissions: verify on the real storage class before the first deploy. When an image runs as a non-root user and owns a persistent volume, set fsGroup to that user's group.

title: Gateway confirms a cancelled match search with a match_cancelled frame
context: Found on the first day in production: after clicking Cancel on the random-chat screen, 'Looking for a match...' stayed on screen. The logs showed matching's CancelMatch returning OK each time (twice, because the screen gave no sign the first click had worked). The gateway's match_cancel handler sent nothing back on success, and the web app sets its searching flag from match_queued and cleared it only on match_found, so nothing ever cleared it after a cancel. The server had removed the caller from the queue; only the screen was wrong, until a reload.
options: Server acknowledgement: the gateway sends a new match_cancelled frame after a successful CancelMatch, and the web app clears its searching flag on it
Client-only: the web app clears its searching flag the moment it sends match_cancel, without waiting for the server
decision: Option 1, chosen by the maintainer. handleMatchCancel enqueues match_cancelled after any successful CancelMatch, whether Cancelled is true or false: false only means the caller was in no queue (already matched, or never queued), so either way they are no longer searching. A failed CancelMatch sends only the error frame. The web reducer's match_cancelled case clears matching and leaves currentMatch alone, so a match_found that raced ahead of the cancel keeps its chat. ARCHITECTURE §5.2's server-to-client table gains the frame.
rationale: It follows DEC-0080, where Next got a match_queued acknowledgement for the same reason: the screen changes only on the server's word, as every other match state in the app does. With the client-only fix, a cancel that failed on the server would show 'not searching' while the caller was still queued, and a match could then appear unannounced. The change is additive: the web reducer's default case ignores unknown frame types, so a page loaded before the release keeps working (it just keeps the old stuck screen).
tradeoffs: One more frame type in the gateway-to-web contract. If the connection drops between the cancel and its acknowledgement, the screen stays on 'Looking for a match...' until the reconnect, as it did before for every cancel.

title: Two more public-launch gates: a frontend rework to the maintainer's instructions, then black-box testing of the frontend against the backend
context: The closed beta has been live on Google Cloud since 2026-10-24 and the web app works end to end, but the maintainer considers the current frontend a placeholder: DEC-0040 deferred a finished visual design, and several things in the UI are not how they should be at launch. The maintainer also wants the product tested the way a student meets it, from the browser, before it is opened to all of KIIT, not only through unit tests, the e2e smoke test and the gateway's own checks.
options: Open to KIIT with the current frontend, and rework and test it after launch
Make the rework and a black-box test launch gates, and open only after both
Keep the current frontend and only add the black-box test
decision: Option 2, chosen by the maintainer on 2026-10-27. (1) Frontend rework: the maintainer will give detailed written instructions for what the UI should be, and the rework follows them exactly rather than extending the current screens by guesswork. (2) Black-box test: after the rework, the product is exercised from the outside through a real browser, covering how the backend reacts to what the frontend sends and how the frontend copes with what the backend returns (errors, reconnects, rate limits, sign-in, moderation, empty and hostile input), written as a test plan with the results committed. Both are added to PLAN.md's Before launch list, ahead of the load test and security review. No launch date is set by this entry.
rationale: A black-box test only means something against the interface students will actually use, so it follows the rework instead of being repeated after it. The rework is also the point at which the contract between web and gateway is most likely to change, which is why a load test number is tied to the commit it was measured on and is rerun before launch if the backend has changed since. Launching on a placeholder UI would put the first impression of the product in front of everyone at once, which the maintainer ruled out.
tradeoffs: The public launch moves later, by however long the rework takes, and its length is not yet known because the instructions have not been given. The closed beta stays closed until then. The test plan and its results add documentation, which AGENTS.md rule 6 asks to keep small, so they live in one committed place rather than several files.

title: Deploy the web app to Vercel only when asked, from a GitHub Actions workflow, instead of on every push through Vercel's Git integration
context: Vercel's GitHub integration builds a preview for every push to every branch and deploys production on every merge to main (its docs: each commit or pull request automatically triggers a new deployment). For this project that meant noise on backend-only pull requests, and a worse problem: when the Cancel fix (DEC-0103) merged, the web app went live while the backend was still the old version, so the screen stayed stuck until the backend was deployed by hand. The web and the backend talk through a contract and must be released backend first. The integration also needed the Vercel GitHub app installed by the organization's owner, which the maintainer's account could not do, and the maintainer's GitHub account was later switched for work reasons.
options: Keep the Git integration and silence it (git.deploymentEnabled for branches other than main, comments off in the dashboard)
Turn the integration off and deploy from a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on merges to main that touch web/
Turn the integration off and deploy from a workflow that only runs when started by hand, after the backend deploy
decision: Option 3, chosen by the maintainer on 2026-10-28. web/vercel.json sets git.deploymentEnabled to false (Vercel's own guide says to do this to avoid duplicate deployments). .github/workflows/web-deploy.yml runs on workflow_dispatch only: it runs the web app's checks (typecheck, tests, build), then pulls the project's settings, builds and deploys with the Vercel CLI (vercel pull, vercel build --prod, vercel deploy --prebuilt --prod), pinned to CLI 64.0.2, using three repository secrets: VERCEL_TOKEN, VERCEL_ORG_ID and VERCEL_PROJECT_ID. The release order is the same as for everything else: merge, GitHub builds the images, deploy the backend with deploy/prod/deploy.sh, confirm, then run Deploy web.
rationale: The web must follow the backend, and a manual trigger makes that order a decision instead of an accident. It matches how the backend is deployed, needs no GitHub app on the organization, and gives Vercel only a token that can deploy this one project, instead of write access to the repository. A failed deploy changes nothing that is live.
tradeoffs: Nothing deploys the web app unless someone remembers to run the workflow, and pull requests no longer get a Vercel preview. A manual preview job could be added. One thing was not verifiable from Vercel's documentation: whether the CLI must run from the repository root or from web/ when the project's Root Directory is set to web; the workflow runs from the root, matching the repo-level link the CLI created, and the first manual run is the test. Vercel's deploy limit on the Hobby plan is 100 per day, far above what this uses.
